Trying to Conceive

Getting fertility help: from the first appointment to a treatment review

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When pregnancy has not happened, the next step is a clear plan, not a promise that one test or medicine will solve everything. Fertility care can move from an initial assessment to selected treatment, specialist advice and repeated decisions about what is worthwhile. These stages help you prepare, but they are not a compulsory ladder: your history, age, findings and preferences may change the order.

1. Decide when to ask for an assessment

For regular unprotected intercourse, ASRM recommends assessment after twelve months when the person providing eggs is younger than 35, and after six months from age 35. Over 40, more immediate advice may be appropriate. Do not wait for these deadlines with irregular or absent periods, suspected endometriosis or tubal disease, a known sperm concern, sexual difficulties or treatment that may affect fertility. Donor conception needs an assessment suited to that route.

Tell the clinician about every previous pregnancy and loss. Two or more miscarriages deserve a discussion about a separate recurrent-loss assessment; they do not have to be consecutive. Even one loss or an ectopic pregnancy may affect the plan according to its circumstances. Local referral routes differ: a family doctor, gynecologist or fertility service may be the entry point. You do not universally need to see one particular specialist first.

2. Prepare a useful first appointment

Bring period dates if available, how long you have been trying, previous pregnancies, operations, infections and test results. List prescribed medicines, over-the-counter products, herbs and supplements for everyone contributing eggs or sperm. Mention painful sex, irregular bleeding, unwanted hair growth, erection or ejaculation difficulties and relevant chronic conditions. Do not delay care to collect six perfect months of tracking.

When a partner contributes sperm, their assessment should usually begin alongside yours. A semen analysis is often an early step, rather than something considered only after every test on the other partner. Write down your main questions and ask for explanations you understand. Reviewing a medicine is not an instruction to stop it; coordinate any changes with its prescriber.

3. Start with tests that answer a question

The initial workup considers ovulation, reproductive anatomy and sperm as appropriate. Menstrual history may be enough to suggest ovulation; selected blood tests, ultrasound and a tubal-patency test may add useful information. A progesterone test, when needed, is timed to the cycle rather than automatically to day 21. Thyroid and prolactin tests need a reason such as relevant symptoms or an ovulation disorder.

An X-ray dye test of the tubes, called HSG, or an ultrasound contrast test may be considered. Laparoscopy, hysteroscopy, genetic tests and endometrial biopsy are not compulsory for everyone. Cervical screening follows the screening programme; infection testing depends on symptoms, risks and planned procedures. Ask what each investigation might change and whether a less invasive approach can answer the same question.

4. Understand what the results do and do not establish

The assessment may identify one factor, several factors or no clear explanation. Unexplained infertility means that standard testing has not found a cause; it does not mean the difficulty is imaginary or that every reproductive process has been proved normal. Request a written summary of completed tests, missing information and the next decision.

AMH and an antral follicle count mainly help estimate ovarian response to stimulation. They do not directly measure egg quality or guarantee a natural pregnancy. An abnormal semen result may need confirmation, with timing guided by its severity and circumstances. Recurrent miscarriage has its own selected investigations, sometimes including pregnancy-tissue testing or assessment of the uterine cavity; it is not a reason to order every available test.

5. Match initial treatment to the diagnosis

An ovulation medicine is not a general pregnancy booster. For selected infertility caused by absent ovulation with PMOS, formerly called PCOS, current international guidance generally favours letrozole; clomiphene or metformin may have roles in particular circumstances. These drugs require a clinical plan and should not be borrowed, combined or increased independently. A person already ovulating with unexplained infertility needs a different discussion.

Surgery may help selected uterine, tubal, endometriosis or sperm-transport problems, but it is not an automatic step before assisted conception. Discuss the likely benefit, recovery time, risks and possible effect on ovarian reserve. Depending on the findings, options may include a defined period of trying, insemination, IVF or other specialist care. There is no single sequence that everyone must complete.

6. Support health while the plan develops

Seek help to stop smoking, avoid alcohol while trying for pregnancy, and discuss recreational drugs and medicines openly. A balanced diet, appropriate activity and folic-acid advice support preparation for pregnancy. If weight is very low or high, ask for realistic nutritional and health support. Changes can matter without guaranteeing conception or making infertility anyone’s fault.

Do not replace timely assessment with a lengthy effort to perfect your lifestyle, especially when age or a known condition makes delay important. Extreme diets and unverified fertility supplements can add risk or expense. Tell the team if tracking, scheduled sex or repeated appointments is affecting sleep, mood or your relationship; support can be part of the plan from the start.

7. Choose specialist care that fits your needs

Specialist referral may be appropriate at the beginning or after initial treatment, depending on the diagnosis and local service. Ask about relevant qualifications, licensing or regulation where you live, available treatments, waiting times and how results are communicated. Opening hours, travel, accessibility, interpreter needs and access to counseling can affect whether care is manageable.

Clinic success rates require context. A live-birth rate is different from a positive-test rate, and a rate per embryo transfer is different from a rate per egg collection or treatment cycle. Age, diagnosis, patient selection and small numbers can make comparisons misleading. Ask for an individualized explanation of likely benefits and uncertainty rather than choosing by the highest advertised percentage alone.

8. Clarify the full cost before committing

Public funding, insurance and private charges vary by place and circumstances. Do not assume everything is uncovered or that an advertised package includes everything you need. Ask for a written, itemized plan covering consultations, tests, medicines, monitoring, procedures and follow-up, with freezing, storage and future embryo-transfer costs where relevant.

Check what the clinic or funder means by a cycle, what happens if treatment is canceled, and which changes could add charges. Include travel and time away from work in your planning. For an optional add-on, ask about evidence of benefit for your situation, risks, alternatives and cost. An expensive extra is not proof of a better chance of a baby.

9. Ask why a test needs repeating

A new clinic should review previous reports before assuming that every investigation must start again. A repeat may be useful if a result was abnormal, circumstances have changed, the earlier test did not answer the current question or a treatment-specific safety check is needed. Ask why it is being repeated and what decision depends on it.

FSH, AMH and an antral follicle count are not interchangeable guarantees of fertility. Repeating AMH routinely just to watch a number change is not the same as using an indicated result to plan treatment. After pregnancy losses, the proposed tests should reflect the loss history and any available tissue results. Share records between services when possible to reduce avoidable duplication and expense.

10. Agree on a written treatment and contact plan

Before starting, clarify the purpose of treatment, expected benefit, important risks, alternatives and the option not to proceed. Ask about medicine names and instructions, required scans or blood tests, appointment timing, consent and whom to contact after hours. With ovarian stimulation, discuss excessive response and multiple-pregnancy risk, including circumstances in which a cycle might be changed or canceled.

Insemination places prepared sperm into the uterus; IVF involves fertilizing retrieved eggs in a laboratory, with an embryo transfer when appropriate. These are different procedures, not inevitable stages for everyone. Make sure you understand what you have consented to, including use or storage of eggs, sperm or embryos when relevant. Keep the clinic’s written instructions available and ask before changing a dose or schedule.

11. Review response rather than repeating treatment indefinitely

Agree in advance when to review the plan and what would prompt an earlier change. After a cycle, discuss what happened, whether the intended biological response occurred, any adverse effects and how the result changes expectations. An unsuccessful cycle does not by itself prove that future pregnancy is impossible, but repeating the same treatment without a review is not a plan.

There is no reliable universal answer to how many months treatment will take. Age, diagnosis, previous response, risks, cost and personal priorities matter. If you need a break, discuss both recovery and any time-sensitive implications rather than assuming a pause is either always harmless or always damaging. A second opinion or counseling may help when the choice to continue, change course or stop feels difficult.

12. Plan the handover after a positive test

Use the clinic’s recommended pregnancy-test date and report the result. Symptoms or early home tests cannot reliably replace its protocol. If you have been prescribed progesterone or other support, follow the clinic’s instructions about continuation and stopping; a positive or negative home test is not a reason to alter treatment yourself.

The team may arrange blood tests or an early scan and then transfer care to a maternity service. Ask who is responsible for follow-up, prescriptions and urgent concerns during that handover. Additional monitoring depends on the treatment, pregnancy findings and your health, including a multiple pregnancy. A positive test is welcome news, but it does not remove the need to assess pain, bleeding or other concerning symptoms.

13. Keep support available if treatment ends

Some people do not achieve a pregnancy with available treatment, and some decide that further treatment is not right for them. Financial limits, medical risks and emotional exhaustion can all shape that decision. Ask for an honest review of the likely benefit of another attempt, without pressure to keep going or an implication that stopping means you did not try hard enough.

A fertility counselor or appropriate peer support can help with grief, differences between partners and decisions about the future. Support remains worthwhile after the last appointment and after a pregnancy begins. You can choose how much to share with relatives or colleagues. Your value and entitlement to care do not depend on a treatment outcome.

14. Know which symptoms should bypass a routine review

During or after fertility treatment, contact the clinic or an urgent medical service promptly for abdominal pain or bloating, nausea or vomiting, feeling faint, coughing blood, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or pain when passing urine or stool. Rapid weight gain or reduced urine also needs prompt advice. Pelvic pain with possible pregnancy, fever or shivering, unusual discharge, blood in urine or stool, or difficulty passing urine or stool needs urgent assessment. Use emergency care instead for any pattern in the next paragraph.

Seek emergency care during or soon after assisted treatment for breathing difficulty, chest or upper-back pain, marked thirst with reduced urine, swelling anywhere in the body, one-sided lower-abdominal pain or shoulder-tip pain. At any stage, pelvic pain that is severe, worsening or painful with movement or touch, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, actual fainting, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty, heavy vaginal bleeding or sudden confusion is an emergency. These can signal ovarian complications, a clot, ectopic pregnancy or another serious condition. Do not wait for several signs, a scheduled test or an appointment, and do not drive yourself.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current ASRM guidance supports timely, selective fertility evaluation and parallel assessment of relevant partners; recurrent loss has its own pathway.

Treatment depends on diagnosis and shared decisions. Clinic outcome figures, ovarian-reserve tests and optional add-ons have limits.

Primary patient guidance supports clear costs, review and follow-up plans, emotional support and prompt assessment of treatment-related warning signs.

How BeMama can help

Keep dates, previous reports, medicines, questions and the next review point together. BeMama can help organize that record; it cannot diagnose infertility, choose treatment or interpret an emergency.

When to seek help

Follow the urgent and emergency guidance above during treatment and possible pregnancy. Do not wait for multiple warning signs or drive yourself to emergency care. Do not start, increase or stop fertility medicines or prescribed hormone support without the treating team’s instructions.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ask for assessment at the appropriate time; known concerns can justify earlier care.
  • Tests and treatment should answer a specific clinical question and consider all relevant contributors.
  • Clarify clinic quality, full costs, consent, monitoring and an after-hours contact before starting.
  • Set review points and discuss the benefit, burden and timing of continuing, changing or pausing treatment.
  • Arrange follow-up after a positive test and ongoing support if treatment ends.

Frequently asked questions

When should I ask for fertility help?

Common ASRM thresholds are twelve months below age 35 and six months from 35, with more immediate advice over 40. Known reproductive concerns or difficulty having sex can justify earlier assessment. Donor-conception pathways need tailored advice.

Should I seek advice after previous miscarriages?

Yes, discuss your pregnancy history. Two or more losses can warrant a recurrent-loss assessment even if they were not consecutive. The circumstances of a single loss or ectopic pregnancy may also affect advice; the appropriate tests are individualized.

Will the first tests always explain why I am not pregnant?

No. Assessment of ovulation, anatomy and sperm may identify a cause, several contributors or unexplained infertility. Ask for a summary of what was established, what remains uncertain and what decision comes next.

Can lifestyle changes replace treatment?

Health support is useful, but it cannot guarantee pregnancy or replace timely assessment. Seek smoking and alcohol support, eat adequately and discuss weight, medicines and folic acid with your clinician. Do not stop prescribed medicines independently.

Does a fertility-clinic referral mean I must have IVF?

No. The appropriate options depend on the findings and your circumstances. They may include a defined period of trying, selected medicines, surgery, insemination or IVF; they are not a compulsory sequence.

Why might a clinic repeat my tests?

Confirmation of an abnormal result, changed circumstances or a treatment-specific requirement may justify it. Ask what the repeat will change and share earlier reports. More testing is not automatically better care.

How long should I continue before reviewing treatment?

Agree on an individual review point before starting, and seek earlier advice for problems. Response, age, diagnosis, risks and priorities determine whether to continue, change or pause. One unsuccessful cycle is not a prediction of every future outcome.

What should I do after a positive treatment-cycle test?

Contact the clinic, follow its medicine instructions and arrange the recommended follow-up and maternity handover. Do not change prescribed hormone support yourself. Pain, bleeding or the urgent symptoms described above need assessment rather than waiting for the next scan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
